intro: The best-preserved ritual of Tunnawiya, the Old Woman: a 'ritual of impurity', also called 'the ritual of the River', for a man or woman who has become impure, including a woman whose children keep dying. Clay is fetched from a riverbank and a spring, objects are held over the patient with incantations, black clothing and wool are stripped off and combed away, the patient passes through gates of hawthorn and alanza-wood, and fertility blessings are spoken to the Sun-god. The colophon, largely restored, marks this as a single complete tablet.

paras.en: Thus (says) Tunnawiya, the Old Woman: If a person, whether a man or a woman, has been placed in some impurity, or someone else has called (him) out (šer ḫalzai-) over impurity, or a woman's children keep dying, or (something) keeps killing(?) her unborn young (šarḫuwant-); (if), whether for a man or for a woman, the limbs are split apart(?) through a matter of impurity,

and that person keeps experiencing (lit. seeing) impurity, then that person, whether man or woman, performs the ritual of impurity as follows. They call it 'the ritual of the River'. This ritual is one and the same (for both).

If (it is) a man, they take a black ram; but if (it is) a woman, they take a black ewe. (Also) one black piglet (and) one black puppy: if (it is) a man, a male piglet; but if a woman, they (are) female. One black shirt, one black išḫiyal- (band), one black kariulli- (hood), one set of black leggings(?), plain(?), one pair of black shoes, [erased: woman's belt], one set of belt (and) TAḪAPŠU-cloth, black. For a woman, (the Old Woman) stops up her ears with black wool.

But if (it is) a man: one black shirt, one set of black leggings(?), and she stops up his ears with black wool. Nine small combs of boxwood, one small šarra- (an implement for 'splitting', perhaps a kind of comb) of boxwood, two black TIYADU (objects of unknown kind), nine soldier-breads, …, six small black pottery(?) utensils, two black braziers, four small black pots, a large black (pot), nine black NAKTAMU-vessels, three black jugs, two black NAMANDU-vessels, two black water jars,

one sheep, one lamb, three warm breads of ḫazzila- (a measure?), one cheese, one sour (bread), one bowl of beer, batter-cake (and) groats, (and) one ḫanišša-vessel of wine for libating. When she has prepared all this, in the evening the Old Woman takes a thin bread, one jug of wine, batter-cake (and) groats, and goes to the riverbank to commission (watarnaḫḫ-) the Mother-goddess of the riverbank.

When she arrives at the riverbank, she breaks one thin bread for the Mother-goddess of the riverbank and places it on the riverbank. She pours batter-cake (and) groats on top, libates wine and speaks:

'O Mother-goddess of the riverbank, see, I have come back to you. This clay, from whichever riverbank it has been taken — you, Mother-goddess of the riverbank, take (it) in your hand, cleanse(?) this ritual patron (lit. 'lord of the ritual') with it, and purify him in (his) twelve limbs!' Then she takes clay of the riverbank. Next she goes to the spring (šakuni-), breaks one thin bread and places it on the mud of the spring. She pours out batter-cake (and) groats, libates wine and speaks:

'Just as you, O spring, keep welling up mud from the dark earth back up (to the surface), so likewise remove evil impurity from this person, from the ritual patron, out of his limbs!' Then she takes clay of the spring. While the Old Woman is fetching these things, reed huts have meanwhile(?) already been made in front of the river. But where do they make them? Where there is no tilled field nearby (and) the [plough] has not reached — there the hut is made.

The Old Woman carries the clay of the riverbank and the clay of the spring there. (From) clay (she makes): twelve tongues of clay, ḫalupant- (meaning unclear) at the back; two oxen of clay; two door-pivots(?) (wawarkima-) of clay. (She takes) a little wool, a little red wool, and a cord [twist]ed of wool and red wool; an eagle's wing; a little bone(?); a little alli- (?); a little seed of the iššarašila-(plant); a little fig; a little zinakki- (?); a little lēši- (?); a piglet of dough; a morsel of wakkešar-bread; a morsel of leavened(?) (bread); a morsel of cucumber(?)-bread; one figurine of wax (and) a figurine of tallow, and these are wrapped in fat. All this she arranges down on a reed tray.

(Also) one fertile(?) (ušantari-) cow; but if (the patron is) a man, she prepares a bull. When it grows light, the ritual patron comes to the hut. When he arrives, he puts on the black (clothes). Then the Old Woman [takes red wool and …s(?) it]

[and throws it up onto (his) body. Then she takes one black sheep and holds it over him, and the Old Woman recites over (him) the incantation of 'holding (over)':] [Luwian incantation, only partly understood: '… Storm-god … up in heaven(?) … run! … heaven(?) … up on earth(?) … run!']
[Afterwards she holds a piglet over him and recites the incantation of the piglet. Afterwards she holds a puppy over him and recites the incantation of the puppy.]

[Afterwards she holds a clay tongue over him and recites the incantation of the tongue. Afterwards she holds the two figurines over him. Afterwards she holds the door-pivot over him. Afterwards she holds the clay oxen over him. Next the dough (piglet), next the cord, next the wing she takes, and waves them away over him. She keeps reciting the incantations; they have already been set down on(?) a tablet.]

[Afterwards she holds the two TIYADU over him and speaks thus: 'Those who with this impurity kept tiyaneš-ing (and) elaneš-ing (two verbs of unknown meaning) his form, bones (and) flesh(?) — now, see, I am tiyaneš-ing (and) elaneš-ing back his form, bones (and) flesh(?) (away from) impurity (and) sorcery(?).' And she places the TIYADU on the tray.]

[Afterwards she holds the figurines of wax (and) of tallow over him and speaks: 'Those who kept making this person impure — now, see, I hold the sorcerers, (as) two figurines, and see, I am tiyaneš-ing (and) elaneš-ing this (person).' Then she melts them down and speaks: 'The persons who, turning evil(?), made (him) impure — let them likewise melt away!']
When she has finished, he rises and washes his hands with wine. Beneath him they hold hot pebbles in a brazier, and she keeps conjuring; (the words) are already recorded(?).

Afterwards he washes himself with water. Beneath him they hold ḫuwalli- (an aromatic substance?) in a brazier, and she keeps conjuring; it is already recorded(?). Afterwards she keeps taking blue wool (and) red wool off his body and keeps speaking thus:

'Those who kept making (him) dark (and) sallow and made (him) impure — whether someone made him impure before the gods, or some dead person made him impure, or someone made him impure before mankind — see, I am performing the ritual of impurity for him,

and I am taking it away from him: from his 12 limbs I take evil impurity, sorcery (and) āštayaratar- (a kind of bewitchment); I take the anger of the god; I take from him the terror of the dead; and I take from him the evil tongue of mankind, of the multitude.' Then she places the blue wool (and) the red wool down on the tray.

Then the black shirt which he is wearing — the Old Woman slits it on him from top to bottom. The black leggings(?) she takes off him over (his) feet; from his ears she takes out the black wool plugs, and speaks thus:

'See, I am taking from him, on account of impurity, the dark (and) the sallow; and I am taking (away) the āštayaratar, the matter of impurity because of which he kept turning dark (and) sallow.' Then she takes off him the dark (things) that he is wearing, and places them down in that place.

Afterwards she waves an empty pot away over him, smashes it and conjures. Then she … (iškar-, lit. 'sticks'?) a ḫupuwai-vessel beneath his feet and speaks: 'See, I am performing the ritual of impurity, and I hold the black sickle(?) of impurity. Let it go: evil impurity, sorcery, āštayaratar, the anger of the gods, the terror of the dead, the ḫuipayata- (meaning unknown) of offspring(?) — let them go!'

Then the ritual patron goes to bathe. The Old Woman sends in nine combs of boxwood (and) sends in one clay figurine, and she places the clay figurine beneath (his) feet for the bathing, and he bathes over (it). As for the combs: the maidservants — each maidservant — comb him once downwards with a comb.
Then the Old Woman speaks thus: 'See, I am sweeping(?) the whole body clean; let evil impurity, sorcery, āštayaratar, the anger of the gods (and) the terror of the dead be combed down from him!'

'See, I hold the šarra-. Whoever with evil impurity kept splitting (him) apart in the 12 limbs — now I keep splitting away from you, from the 12 limbs, evil impurity, sorcery, āštayaratar, the anger of the gods (and) the terror of the dead; let it be split away from him!'

Then the combs, the šarra-, the wing, the shirt, the black [leggings(?)] — whatever was on him — she afterwards releases into the river. They bring the kuptar- (meaning unknown) down, and the figurine too, and [throw(?)] it into the river.

They carry the puppy (and) the piglet to an uncultivated place and burn them [with fi]re. While … , the Old Woman [make]s (a gate) of hawthorn at the [up]per side of the hut and [bind]s it on top with white wool.

[On the fro]nt side she [scat]ters three thick loaves (and) groats(?) […], and on this side she makes a gate of alanza-(wood) […], binds (it) with black wool […], (and) places [groa]ts likewise […] they arrange […] … they come(?) to the place […] she keeps [pronoun]cing(?) […]
[…] … the pure hut […] [o]r a woman […] the hawthorn gate […] she speaks:

'[…] white(?) […]; [in blood-re]d you clothe (yourself). The sheep(?) passes down beneath you and you pull its wool from it; the o[x] passes down beneath [you] and you pull its šukšuka- (tuft of hair?) from it.

Likewise pull away from this ritual patron evil impurity, sorcery, āštayaratar, the anger of the gods, the oath (lit. 'life of the god'), the tongue of the multitude (and) the shortened year!' Then he throws(?) the thin bread back, and the Old Woman speaks: 'Let the grain(?) turn his evil impurity away behind (him)!'

Next he goes out beneath the alanza-gate, and she speaks: 'Just as this alanza- keeps purifying thousands (and) ten thousands(?) of shepherds (and) cowherds, so likewise purify this ritual patron in the 12 limbs of evil impurity, sorcery, āštayaratar, the oath, evil dreams, the anger of the gods (and) the terror of the dead!' Then he throws(?) the thin bread back; the Old Woman speaks exactly the same.
She goes to the riverbank, breaks one thin bread at the riverbank, places it down on the riverbank (and) pours out batter-cake (and) groats.

She libates wine once and speaks: 'O Mother-goddess of the riverbank, see, the 12 limbs (that were) impure have been cleansed (and) purified by your hand.' Next she goes to the spring, breaks one thin bread, pours out batter-cake (and) groats, libates wine once and speaks: 'O Sun-god, my lord, see, the 12 limbs have been cleansed with the clay of the spring (and) purified.'

Then she takes the fertile(?) cow by the horn and speaks: 'O Sun-god, my lord, just as this cow is fertile (ušantari-), and she (stands) in the fertile pen and keeps filling the pen with bulls (and) cows — see, let the ritual patron likewise be fertile, and let him likewise fill (his) house with sons, daughters, grandchildren, great-grandchildren (and) descendants upon descendants!' Then [they drive it back to the pen].

Where a tree stands clothed (with) fruit, she goes there and takes hold of it (and speaks): 'O Sun-god, my lord, just as this tree is clo[thed] (with fruit), (and) just as it has driven up (its) tarša- (shoots?), and life, health, vi[gour] … grandchildren(?) … […] — so let the ritual patron likewise be clothed (with) grandchildren (and) great-grandchildren!'
Then he [steps(?)] opposite the Sun-god […], libates to the Sun-god and speaks: 'O Sun-god, eat! See, the 12 limbs (are) cleansed by the word of the Sun-god(?). You, Sun-god, keep (him) released(?)!'

Then three warm breads, one cheese, [cook]ed liver (and) heart […] or wine […] (she) goes to the (deified) Hut(?) […] and (to) the Mother-goddess of the riverbank […] she speaks thus: '[…] Eat! And with [you …] let (him) eat! From which […] this ritual patron […]'

'[…] they have purified the 12 limbs […] offspring(?) […]' And on (it) the liv[er …] or she libates wine three times […]. He drinks (to) the River three times; afterwards [(to) the riverbank(?) he drinks three times. Then he drives up into the city.]
[Colophon:] [One tablet of the ritual of impurity and of the River. This (is) the ritual of Tunnawiya, the Old Woman; complete. Pikku wrote (it).]
